caption:
Just because a treatment is trending doesn’t mean it’s the right treatment for you.

Sculptra has seen a significant rise in popularity, driven in part by the growing conversation around collagen stimulation and “regenerative” aesthetics.

But trends can oversimplify something that should always be highly individualized.

In aesthetic medicine, the question shouldn’t be “What treatment is everyone getting?” It should be “What is actually causing the change I’m trying to correct?”

Volume loss, s
transcript: Hi everyone, I wanted to address really my opinion about use of sculpture. Sculpture is having a major moment on social media right now and whenever I see an aesthetic treatment become a trend, I really get concerned. Really your face should never be treated according to what happens to be popular this year. Sculpture is polyelactic acid, which is powdered suture. Unlike a traditional hyaluronic acid filler, it works by creating a tissue response that stimulates your body to produce collagen, but that's really a type of collagen that leads to scarring. That is why precisely I personally take a very conservative approach to using sculpture. We now know that inflammatory reactions, nodules, scarring occur with these bio stimulators like sculpture, but not with hyaluronic acid. We're now having an interesting conversation with facial surgery about what repeated bio stimulatory treatments with sculpture can really eventually lead to issues when someone needs a facelift down the line. Recent survey of facial surgeons found that many report greater difficulty operating on patients who've had sculpture and bio stimulatory treatments such as difficulty dissecting the tissue, longer operating times, changes in planning for surgery. That study wasn't specifically about sculpture alone. It doesn't mean that everyone who has sculpture is going to have a surgical complication, but I think it's something patients deserve to know and something we need to continue studying. I find people who are doing sculpture really at an early age, and what those things are repeatedly with sculpture, you can have problems in your 50s and 60s when it comes to surgical intervention. For me, aesthetic medicine is really about thinking long term down the line. You can choose something that's being injected into your face simply because it's viral. Ask what it does, ask what the potential complications are, ask whether there's an alternative, and most importantly, ask whether you actually need it, rely on a trusted provider who's had years of experience, trends really come and go, but your face deserves a long term plan. So I hope that helps. Thank you.

title: Why Tretinoin Stops Working
caption:
Does tretinoin really stop working over time? Dermatologist Dr. Dray explains why your skin becoming more tolerant of tretinoin does not necessarily mean the retinoid has stopped working.

If acne comes back while using tretinoin, there may be other explanations, including changes in hormones, acne severity, skincare routines, or how consistently the medication is being used. Tretinoin and other topical retinoids can also be used as maintenance treatments to help prevent acne from returning.

Dr
transcript: What's the deal? Why is my tretinoin no longer working? Did my skin become resistant to it? This is something a lot of people end up encountering when it comes to using a topical retinoid. The benefits that they observed in the beginning, maybe they've observed them for a while. All of a sudden, it doesn't cut it in. Your acne, it's breaking out. So does this stop working? No. Topical retinoids do not stop working. Nor does your skin develop tolerance to or resistance against. Topical retinoids work by binding to certain receptors and skin cells and influencing the genes that are expressed, ultimately playing a role in how they act. And that doesn't change with ongoing use. What is more likely is that your skin condition is no longer well controlled by this topical alone. In the case of acne, this is not actually unusual. Acne is influenced by your hormones, which can change throughout your lifetime. It doesn't mean that this stop working. It just means that perhaps you need to see your dermatologist because maybe you need additional treatment in order to now exert control above and beyond a topical retinoid.
